{{Short description|Stochastic way of assigning quantities across a space}}
In [[probability theory]], a '''random measure''' is a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]]-valued [[random element]].<ref name="RN"/><ref name="G"/> Random measures are for example used in the theory of [[random process]]es, where they form many important [[point process]]es such as [[Poisson point process]]es and [[Cox process]]es.

== Definition ==
Random measures can be defined as [[transition kernel]]s or as [[random element]]s. Both definitions are equivalent. For the definitions, let <math> E </math> be a [[Separable space|separable]] [[complete metric space]] and let <math> \mathcal E </math> be its [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel <math> \sigma </math>-algebra]]. (The most common example of a separable complete metric space is <math> \R^n </math>.)
=== As a transition kernel ===
A random measure <math> \zeta </math> is a ([[almost surely|a.s.]]) [[Locally finite measure|locally finite]] [[transition kernel]] from an abstract [[probability space]] <math> (\Omega, \mathcal A, P) </math> to <math> (E, \mathcal E) </math>.<ref name="Kallenberg1" />

Being a transition kernel means that
*For any fixed <math> B \in \mathcal \mathcal E </math>, the mapping
:<math> \omega \mapsto \zeta(\omega,B) </math>
:is [[measurable function|measurable]] from <math> (\Omega, \mathcal A) </math>  to <math> (\R, \mathcal B(\R)) </math>
*For every fixed <math> \omega \in \Omega </math>, the mapping
:<math> B \mapsto \zeta(\omega, B)  \quad (B \in \mathcal E)</math>
:is a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] on <math> (E, \mathcal E) </math>

Being locally finite means that the measures
:<math> B \mapsto \zeta(\omega, B) </math>
satisfy <math> \zeta(\omega,\tilde B) < \infty </math> for all bounded measurable sets <math> \tilde B \in \mathcal E </math>
and for all <math> \omega \in \Omega </math> except some <math> P </math>-[[null set]]

In the context of [[Stochastic process|stochastic processes]] there is the related concept of a [[Markov kernel|stochastic kernel, probability kernel, Markov kernel]]'''.'''

=== As a random element ===
Define
:<math> \tilde \mathcal  M:= \{ \mu \mid \mu \text{ is measure on } (E, \mathcal E) \} </math>

and the subset of locally finite measures by
:<math> \mathcal M:= \{ \mu \in \tilde \mathcal M \mid \mu(\tilde B) < \infty \text{ for all bounded measurable } \tilde B \in \mathcal E \} </math>

For all bounded measurable <math> \tilde B </math>, define the mappings
:<math> I_{\tilde B } \colon \mu \mapsto \mu(\tilde B)  </math>

from <math> \tilde \mathcal M </math> to <math> \R </math>. Let <math> \tilde \mathbb M </math> be the <math> \sigma </math>-algebra induced by the mappings <math> I_{\tilde B } </math> on <math> \tilde \mathcal M </math> and <math> \mathbb M </math> the <math> \sigma </math>-algebra induced by the mappings <math> I_{\tilde B } </math>  on <math> \mathcal M </math>. Note that <math> \tilde\mathbb M|_{\mathcal M}= \mathbb M </math>.

A random measure is a random element from <math> (\Omega, \mathcal A, P) </math> to <math> (\tilde \mathcal M, \tilde \mathbb M) </math> that almost surely takes values in <math> (\mathcal M, \mathbb M) </math><ref name="Kallenberg1" /><ref name="Klenke526" /><ref name="daleyPPI2003"/>

== Basic related concepts ==
=== Intensity measure ===
{{main article|intensity measure}}
For a random measure <math> \zeta</math>, the measure <math> \operatorname E \zeta </math> satisfying
:<math> \operatorname E \left[ \int f(x) \; \zeta (\mathrm dx )\right] = \int f(x) \; \operatorname E \zeta (\mathrm dx)</math>

for every positive measurable function <math> f </math> is called the intensity measure of <math> \zeta </math>. The intensity measure exists for every random measure and is a [[s-finite measure]].

=== Supporting measure ===
For a random measure <math> \zeta</math>, the measure <math> \nu </math> satisfying
:<math> \int f(x) \; \zeta(\mathrm dx )=0 \text{ a.s. } \text{ iff } \int f(x) \; \nu (\mathrm dx)=0</math>

for all positive measurable functions is called the '''supporting measure''' of <math> \zeta</math>. The supporting measure exists for all random measures and can be chosen to be finite.

=== Laplace transform ===
For a random measure <math> \zeta</math>, the [[Laplace transform]] is defined as
:<math> \mathcal L_\zeta(f)= \operatorname E \left[ \exp \left( -\int f(x) \; \zeta (\mathrm dx ) \right) \right]</math>

for every positive measurable function <math> f </math>.

== Basic properties ==
=== Measurability of integrals ===
For a random measure <math> \zeta </math>, the integrals
:<math> \int f(x) \zeta(\mathrm dx) </math>
and
<math> \zeta(A) := \int \mathbf 1_A(x) \zeta(\mathrm dx)  </math>

for positive <math> \mathcal E </math>-measurable <math> f </math> are measurable, so they are [[random variable]]s.

=== Uniqueness ===
The distribution of a random measure is uniquely determined by the distributions of
:<math> \int f(x) \zeta(\mathrm dx) </math>

for all continuous functions with compact support <math> f </math> on <math> E </math>. For a fixed [[semiring]] <math> \mathcal I \subset \mathcal E </math> that generates <math> \mathcal E </math> in the sense that <math> \sigma(\mathcal I)=\mathcal E </math>, the distribution of a random measure is also uniquely determined by the integral over all positive [[simple function|simple]] <math> \mathcal I </math>-measurable functions <math> f </math>.<ref name="Kallenberg52" />

=== Decomposition ===
A measure generally might be decomposed as:
:<math> \mu=\mu_d + \mu_a = \mu_d + \sum_{n=1}^N \kappa_n \delta_{X_n}, </math>
Here <math>\mu_d</math> is a diffuse measure without atoms, while <math>\mu_a</math> is a purely atomic measure.

==Random counting measure==
A random measure of the form:

:<math> \mu=\sum_{n=1}^N \delta_{X_n}, </math>

where <math>\delta</math> is the [[Dirac measure]] and <math>X_n</math> are random variables, is called a ''[[point process]]''<ref name="RN"/><ref name="G"/> or '''random counting measure'''. This random measure describes the set of ''N'' particles, whose locations are given  by the (generally vector valued) random variables <math>X_n</math>. The diffuse component <math>\mu_d</math> is null for a counting measure.

In the formal notation of above a random counting measure is a map from a probability space to the [[measurable space]] {{nowrap|(<math>N_X</math>,&thinsp;<math>\mathfrak{B}(N_X)</math>)}}. Here <math>N_X</math> is the space of all boundedly finite integer-valued measures <math>N \in M_X</math> (called [[counting measure]]s). 

The definitions of expectation measure, Laplace functional, moment measures and stationarity for random measures follow those of [[point process]]es. Random measures are useful in the description and analysis of [[Monte Carlo method]]s, such as [[numerical quadrature#Monte Carlo|Monte Carlo numerical quadrature]] and [[particle filter]]s.<ref name="crisan" />
